\section[a prova]{a prova — the proof, the evidence; the test}

\label{lesson:PT-C341-prova}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for absurd, then the Portuguese for debatable.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a prova}
\textbf{a prova} — \textquotedblleft{}the proof, the evidence; the test\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Não há nenhuma prova de que ele mentiu.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is no proof that he lied.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Uma prova} can also be a test at school. \emph{À prova de água} — waterproof.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{prova} is built on \emph{provar} \textquotedblleft{}to prove, to try\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{probāre} \textquotedblleft{}to test, to approve, to prove\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short); Old Portuguese already had \emph{prova} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a prova}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a prova}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a prova}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for absurd, then the Portuguese for debatable, then say \emph{a prova} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does a prova mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The proof, the evidence; the test\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[evidente]{evidente — evident, clear}

\label{lesson:PT-C341-evidente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for debatable, then the Portuguese for the proof.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: evidente}
\textbf{evidente} — \textquotedblleft{}evident, clear\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
É evidente que ele está cansado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is evident that he is tired.}
\end{quote}

\emph{É evidente que} takes the indicative. \emph{Evidentemente} — evidently.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{evidente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ēvidēns} \textquotedblleft{}visible, apparent, clear\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{vidēre} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{evidente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{evidente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{evidente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for debatable, then the Portuguese for the proof, then say \emph{evidente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does evidente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Evident, clear\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[óbvio]{óbvio — obvious}

\label{lesson:PT-C341-obvio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the proof, then the Portuguese for evident.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: óbvio}
\textbf{óbvio} — \textquotedblleft{}obvious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A resposta parecia óbvia a toda a gente.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The answer seemed obvious to everyone.}
\end{quote}

\emph{É óbvio!} — obviously! \emph{Obviamente} — obviously.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{óbvio} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{obvius} \textquotedblleft{}in the way, meeting, easy to find\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{ob} \textquotedblleft{}towards\textquotedblright{} and \emph{via} \textquotedblleft{}road\textquotedblright{}: it lies right in your path.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{óbvio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{óbvio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{óbvio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the proof, then the Portuguese for evident, then say \emph{óbvio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does óbvio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Obvious\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[indiscutível]{indiscutível — indisputable, beyond question}

\label{lesson:PT-C341-indiscutivel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for evident, then the Portuguese for obvious.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: indiscutível}
\textbf{indiscutível} — \textquotedblleft{}indisputable, beyond question\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O talento dela é indiscutível.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Her talent is beyond question.}
\end{quote}

The opposite of \emph{discutível}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{indiscutível} is built from the prefix \emph{in-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} and \emph{discutível} \textquotedblleft{}debatable\textquotedblright{}, on the verb \emph{discutir}, which comes from Latin \emph{discutere} \textquotedblleft{}to strike asunder\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indiscutível}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{indiscutível}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{indiscutível}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for evident, then the Portuguese for obvious, then say \emph{indiscutível} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does indiscutível mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Indisputable, beyond question\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[refutar]{refutar — to refute, to disprove}

\label{lesson:PT-C341-refutar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for obvious, then the Portuguese for indisputable.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: refutar}
\textbf{refutar} — \textquotedblleft{}to refute, to disprove\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A cientista refutou a teoria com dados novos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The scientist refuted the theory with new data.}
\end{quote}

Formal. \emph{Refutar um argumento} — to refute an argument.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{refutar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{refūtāre} \textquotedblleft{}to check, to drive back, to repress\textquotedblright{}, and so \textquotedblleft{}to disprove\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
